title: Issues Stack Up With More HBM Layers
gist: HBM (high-bandwidth memory) scaling is hitting hard physical limits — thinner dies, TSV area overhead, and thermal bottlenecks — while HBM's roughly 3x higher wafer consumption per bit versus standard DRAM is a root cause of the broader DRAM shortage; Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix data from Hot Chips 2026 show DRAM/HBM bandwidth scaling (2x/2 years) is falling behind AI compute demand growth (3x/2 years), widening the 'memory wall.'

insights.claim: Stacking more DRAM layers into an HBM module requires thinning the dies to stay within the fixed package height limit, but die thinning is approaching a physical breaking point, making dies harder to handle in manufacturing, more prone to warpage, and more difficult to align and bond.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Physical die-thinning limits directly constrain how much further HBM stack heights can scale, implying diminishing returns and rising yield risk for next-generation HBM generations (e.g., HBM4 and beyond) — a yield/cost risk for memory suppliers and their AI-chip customers (Nvidia, AMD, hyperscalers).
insights.quote: thinning DRAM dies is reaching the breaking point — sometimes literally. They are harder to handle during manufacturing and packaging.

insights.claim: Through-silicon vias (TSVs), the main data paths in HBM's wide parallel interface, create a direct area-versus-bandwidth tradeoff: more TSVs increase bandwidth but consume silicon area that would otherwise store memory cells, and taller stacks make heat dissipation from the base logic die harder.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Explains the structural ceiling on HBM density improvements — bandwidth gains are being purchased at the direct expense of storage capacity and thermal headroom, a key mechanism for modeling future HBM generation cost/performance tradeoffs.
insights.quote: The more TSVs, the greater the bandwidth, which is fundamental for improving the performance of any HBM module. But TSVs also consume area on a die, which limits the amount of data that can actually be stored on each layer.

insights.claim: HBM consumes significantly more silicon and wafer capacity per bit than conventional DRAM even though it uses the same underlying commoditized DRAM cell technology, and HBM yields only about one-third the gigabytes per wafer that standard DDR DRAM achieves.
insights.speaker: Jim Handy, general director at Objective Analysis
insights.so_what: Quantifies the root economic cause of the DRAM shortage: every HBM bit produced consumes roughly 3x the wafer capacity of a standard DRAM bit, meaning AI-driven HBM demand growth mechanically squeezes supply of all DRAM types (including commodity DRAM used in PCs/phones) — a direct read-through to expect continued/worsening DRAM pricing pressure across the entire memory market, benefiting Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix pricing power.
insights.quote: If you look at the number of gigabytes you get per wafer, it's a third as much as what you get with DDR — standard DRAM... HBM just is demanding a colossal number of wafers, and that's causing all DRAM to go into shortage
insights.locator: Jim Handy quote on wafer area

themes.theme: Root causes of the DRAM shortage

insights.claim: Jim Handy identified three specific causes of the current DRAM shortage: explosive AI-driven demand for extremely fast DRAM, reduced availability of DRAM wafers because HBM consumes more wafer capacity than other DRAM types, and insufficient manufacturing capacity to keep pace with demand.
insights.speaker: Jim Handy, general director at Objective Analysis
insights.so_what: A structured three-factor framework for diagnosing the DRAM shortage that investors can use to assess whether the shortage is cyclical (capacity catch-up) or structural (persistent AI demand + technical wafer-intensity of HBM).
insights.quote: Explosive AI demand and unprecedented spending are increasing demand for extremely fast DRAM; Reduced availability of DRAM wafers because HBM requires more than other flavors of DRAM, and Insufficient manufacturing capacity to keep pace with insatiable demand.
insights.locator: Jim Handy's three reasons for DRAM shortages

insights.claim: DRAM manufacturers were caught off guard by the AI-driven demand surge because for over a decade prior, DRAM makers had been able to match market growth simply by increasing gigabytes-per-wafer efficiency, so they had not added new fab capacity in more than 10 years.
insights.speaker: Jim Handy, general director at Objective Analysis
insights.so_what: Explains why the current DRAM supply response is slow and lagged: a 10+ year capacity-expansion drought means new fabs (which take at least a couple of years to build) are only now breaking ground, implying the DRAM shortage and elevated pricing could persist for multiple years before new capacity comes fully online — a bullish multi-year setup for memory makers' margins and capex suppliers.
insights.quote: They hadn't added capacity for over 10 years, and all of a sudden they're having to add factories.

insights.claim: Building a new DRAM fab takes at least a couple of years, with timelines varying by region depending on power, water, environmental regulation, and labor availability, and it is not clear that current construction plans will be sufficient to meet demand and bring DRAM prices back down.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic multi-year timeline (2+ years minimum) before DRAM supply normalizes, meaning elevated DRAM/HBM pricing is likely to persist near-term — relevant for forecasting Micron/Samsung/SK hynix earnings and for AI-hardware cost inputs (Nvidia/AMD GPU bill-of-materials).
insights.quote: it takes at least a couple years to build a new DRAM fab... it's not at all clear whether the current construction will be sufficient to meet demand and bring DRAM prices back in line.

insights.claim: Memory demand is accelerating faster than compute demand: compute is scaling at roughly 3x every 2 years while HBM bandwidth is scaling at only about 2x every 2 years, meaning the 'memory wall' problem is getting worse, not better.
insights.speaker: Raghu Sreeramaneni, fellow for HBM Design Architecture at Micron
insights.so_what: A concrete, quotable growth-rate gap (3x/2yr compute vs. 2x/2yr HBM bandwidth) that quantifies the widening memory wall — a structural, multi-year tailwind for memory pricing power and a headwind for AI accelerator performance scaling that investors should factor into GPU/AI-chip performance roadmap expectations.
insights.quote: Compute is scaling at roughly 3X every 2 years... HBM, while it has solved a lot of the bandwidth issues and scaled up bandwidth, is lagging and is more like 2X every 2 years. So the memory wall is still present, and in fact, it may be getting worse.
insights.locator: Sreeramaneni quote on compute vs. memory scaling

insights.claim: HBM's primary appeal is enabling effectively very large, very fast cache-like memory near the processor since building an equivalently large SRAM cache would be prohibitively expensive; HBM achieves high bandwidth via very wide buses at roughly the same latency as standard DRAM.
insights.speaker: Jim Handy, general director at Objective Analysis
insights.so_what: Clarifies why HBM is the industry's chosen solution over alternatives like massive SRAM — informs why HBM demand (and its cost pressures) is structurally tied to AI accelerator design, not a passing trend.
insights.quote: everybody would like to have an infinitely large cache memory on their processor chip... They can't have that, so they say, 'Okay, how about if we have a huge SRAM? That's way too expensive. And so they use HBM.

insights.claim: HBM bandwidth has essentially doubled with each generation, driven primarily by increasing the number of TSVs (since increasing TSV signaling speed is difficult and risky) rather than scaling TSV speed itself, but this forces continuous reduction in TSV pitch, consuming more die area; HBM3E has 128 banks per DRAM die while HBM4 goes up to 256 banks per die.
insights.speaker: Sangwook Han, design team member in Samsung's Memory Business
insights.so_what: Specific generational data points (128 vs. 256 banks) quantify the pace of HBM architectural scaling and clarify that Samsung's approach relies on TSV count growth (area cost) rather than speed scaling — useful detail for modeling die-area and cost-per-bit trends across HBM generations.
insights.quote: HBM3E had 128 banks on every DRAM die. HBM4 goes all the way to 256 banks per DRAM die

insights.claim: Scaling the PHY I/O in the base die is much more complicated than scaling TSVs, making it the harder of the two major bandwidth bottlenecks in HBM design.
insights.speaker: Sangwook Han, design team member in Samsung's Memory Business
insights.so_what: Identifies base-die PHY I/O design as the harder, less-solved engineering bottleneck relative to TSV scaling — a technical area to watch for differentiation among HBM base-die suppliers/foundries (e.g., those partnering with Samsung/SK hynix/Micron on base logic dies).
insights.quote: To achieve higher bandwidth, we face two major bottlenecks — TSVs between dies and the PHY I/O in the base die... compared to TSVs, scaling of the PHY I/O is much more complicated.

insights.claim: SK hynix's 16-high HBM development is increasing total cube thickness from 720 to 775 microns to gain manufacturing margin, but must still reduce die thickness by 10% compared to the 12-die-high generation, reduce gap height by 50%, and reduce bump pitch — creating new die-wall-thinning, power-density, and thermal challenges from the added oxide layers per die.
insights.speaker: Jaesik Lee, vice president of package engineering at SK hynix America
insights.so_what: Concrete engineering specs (720→775 microns, 10% thickness reduction, 50% gap-height reduction) for SK hynix's next HBM generation show the fine-margin engineering trade-offs required to hit higher stack counts — relevant for assessing SK hynix's execution risk and timeline for 16-high HBM commercialization.
insights.quote: There is discussion about increasing the total cube thickness from 720 to 775 microns... but we still need to reduce the thickness by 10% compared to the 12-die height.

insights.claim: In an HBM cube, the base die is typically the hottest component due to its high-speed interconnections and complex logic, yet the heat sink sits at the top of the stack, creating a thermal resistance path through the entire cube; DRAM reliability suffers (via increased refresh problems) when it overheats, and thermal considerations are now driving architecture decisions rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: Raghu Sreeramaneni, fellow for HBM Design Architecture at Micron
insights.so_what: A notable inversion — 'architecting solutions around thermals instead of the other way around' — signals thermal management has become a first-order design constraint for HBM, which favors suppliers of advanced thermal/packaging solutions (hybrid bonding, better heat sinks) serving the AI memory supply chain.
insights.quote: The base die is typically the hottest part of the die... Your heat sink and cooling is at the very top. There is thermal resistance through the cube... we are now architecting solutions around thermals instead of the other way around.

insights.claim: Future HBM/interposer innovation will need new high-speed I/O approaches such as memory-optimized SerDes PHYs (versus native memory interfaces), with optics eventually entering this space, alongside rapid interposer innovation to fit bigger systems-in-package with more GPUs and HBM using different materials.
insights.speaker: Raghu Sreeramaneni, fellow for HBM Design Architecture at Micron
insights.so_what: Points to optical interconnects and advanced SerDes/interposer technology as the next investable frontier for scaling memory-to-processor bandwidth beyond current HBM architectures — a forward signal for optics/photonics and advanced-packaging suppliers to the AI data center chain.
insights.quote: We are looking at more memory-optimized SerDes PHYs, instead of more native memory interfaces... Optics is eventually going to come into this space, as well.

insights.claim: Most current HBM bonding uses thermal-compression bonding or microbumps, but the industry will transition to fusion bonding and hybrid bonding, which support single-digit-micron pitch resolution, move more data through the package, and improve thermal performance because fewer dielectric layers sit between dies.
insights.speaker: Raghu Sreeramaneni, fellow for HBM Design Architecture at Micron
insights.so_what: Identifies hybrid/fusion bonding as the next bonding-technology transition for HBM, benefiting both bandwidth and thermal performance simultaneously — a specific technology to track for advanced-packaging equipment vendors (e.g., bonding equipment makers) serving HBM supply chains.
insights.quote: At some point there is a transition to move into more fusion bonding and hybrid bonding, which can support extremely tight pitches with single-digit micron resolution, and which can move much more data through the package.

insights.claim: As AI adoption grows across data centers and edge devices, the likely solution to memory-bandwidth constraints is more distributed processing — including in-memory and in-sensor processing at the edge — reducing how much data must be sent from edge devices to AI data centers for generative and agentic AI workloads.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Suggests a structural shift toward edge/in-memory compute and smaller language models as a workaround to the memory wall, rather than pure HBM scaling — a thesis relevant for edge-AI chip and in-memory-compute startups as a longer-term alternative investment theme to pure HBM capacity plays.
insights.quote: The solution will likely be more distributed processing of that data, including in-memory and in-sensor processing at the edge, and less data being sent from the edge to AI data centers

insights.claim: HBM scaling is evolving from a pure memory-density problem into a system-level problem: adding more dies to boost bandwidth creates cascading challenges in die thickness, thermal management, and package complexity, and will almost certainly reduce yield.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A summary causal thesis: expect continued yield pressure (and thus tighter/costlier supply) as HBM stack heights increase, reinforcing a bullish pricing/margin outlook for HBM suppliers able to solve these system-level integration problems (Micron, SK hynix, Samsung) versus those that cannot.
insights.quote: HBM scaling is evolving from a memory density problem to a system-level one... it almost certainly will reduce yield.
